title: Overloaded Pieces
subtitle: A defender with two jobs is doing neither.
goals: Identify a piece that is defending two things at once
Offer material on squares the overloaded piece cannot accept
Play an eleven-ply combination from a real master game

steps.say: New Orleans, 1920. Edwin Adams against Carlos Torre — one of the most famous combinations ever played, and it is nothing but this single idea repeated five times. Look at Black's back rank: the rook on e8 is defended only by the queen on d7. And your rooks are doubled on the e-file. Black's queen has two jobs: guard the e8 rook, and stay safe. You're White.

Before the fireworks, count it. If Black's queen ever leaves the defence of e8 — or is captured — then Rxe8+ Rxe8 Rxe8 is mate on the back rank. That single fact is the engine of the whole combination: every white queen move from here is a free offer, and Black can never accept.

autoMoves.say: Just to see it: Rxe8+ forces Rxe8...
...and Rxe8+ would be mate, except that here the queen on d7 is still guarding e8 and simply recaptures. So the goal is clear: get rid of that queen without letting it take anything.

steps.prompt: Black's queen is overloaded — it guards e8 and cannot leave. Hound it off the board. Six queen moves, one pawn move, and Black is lost.
hints: Attack the black queen with your own queen, on a square where capturing it loses to Rxe8+ Rxe8 Rxe8#.
Qg4! is the first offer: Qxg4 allows the back-rank mate. Black must decline and keep guarding e8 — every square the queen finds, attack it again.
Qg4 Qb5, Qc4 Qd7, Qc7 Qb5, then a4! drives it once more, and Re4 seals the file before Qxb7 finishes.

line.say: Offer number one. 18...Qxg4 loses to Rxe8+ Rxe8 Rxe8#, so the queen must run — and it must run to a square that still defends e8.
Offer number two, attacking the queen again. Taking still loses to the same back-rank mate.
Offer number three — the queen sits right next to Black's, completely en prise, and still cannot be taken.
A quiet pawn move, and the cruellest one: the queen is attacked by a PAWN and still cannot take anything or leave the e8 rook.
Offer number four, this time with a rook — and the rook stays on the e-file while it attacks. Black's queen has run out of safe squares that also guard e8.

And the last one. Black resigned here: the queen cannot take on b7 because of Rxe8+ Rxe8 Rxe8#, and it can no longer hold both the b7 pawn and the e8 rook. Every single white move in this combination was a piece hanging on purpose.

rejections.say: The mate is real but the order is wrong: after Rxe8+ Rxe8 Rxe8+ the queen simply recaptures on e8 and you've traded everything for nothing. First DEFLECT the queen — attack it on squares where taking allows that same mate.
Attacking the queen is the right idea, but a4 lets Black answer Qxa4 straight away with no back-rank problem, because your queen isn't protected by the mate threat there. The square is g4.
Close, but Black replies axb4 — you've hung the queen to a pawn for nothing. Choose a square where the capture loses to the back-rank mate: g4.
Bringing another piece in looks natural, but it lets Black untangle with ...dxe5 or ...Rxe5. The combination is purely about the overloaded queen — attack it directly and never stop.

steps.wrongSay: Black's queen cannot leave e8 undefended, and it cannot capture anything that allows Rxe8+ Rxe8 Rxe8#. Attack it with your queen on a square protected by that threat.
steps.successSay: Adams-Torre, 1920. White offered the queen on five different squares and Black could not take it once. That is what 'overloaded' means.

steps.say: The habit to build from this: when you're looking for a combination, don't start by asking 'what can I take?'. Ask 'which enemy piece is doing two jobs?'. Then attack it, or take one of the things it guards. A defender that must stay where it is has stopped being a piece and become a target.
